ch01.anchor: Selected Historical and Cultural Materials of Shanghai
ch01.note: The wenshi ziliao (‘cultural and historical materials’) series, part of a nationwide project begun in 1959 under the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference—the CPPCC, the People’s Republic’s united-front advisory body. Committees at every level gathered memoirs from surviving participants in pre-1949 life—former officials, officers, businessmen, and, as here, gang members—to preserve first-hand material. The genre is candid but shaped by its moment: written under an official frame, the volumes mix valuable eyewitness detail with the political vocabulary of their day.

ch01.anchor: The names Green Gang and Hong Gang
ch01.note: The two great secret-society brotherhoods of the Chinese underworld. The Green Gang (青帮, Qingbang), grown from the Grand Canal grain-transport guilds, dominated Shanghai. The Hong Gang (洪帮)—also the Hongmen (洪门), loosely the ‘Red Gang’—was the sworn-brotherhood network of south China descended from the anti-Qing Triads. As the note concedes, the writers here name them inconsistently, and this translation keeps each writer’s usage.

ch02.note: The standard frame of Chinese Marxist historiography for the century from the Opium War (1840) to 1949: China as ‘semi-colonial’ (dominated by foreign powers through treaty ports and concessions rather than formally colonized) and ‘semi-feudal’ (its landlord-peasant order eroded but not replaced). The preface reads the gangs through this lens throughout.

The Small Sword Society (小刀会), a Triad-linked secret society, seized the walled Chinese city of Shanghai in September 1853 and held it seventeen months before the Qing retook it in February 1855. Overlapping the Taiping war, it is treated in official history as an early anti-feudal, anti-imperialist revolt.

The purge of 12 April 1927, when Chiang Kai-shek turned on his Communist allies in Shanghai. Green Gang gunmen—marshalled with Du Yuesheng, Huang Jinrong, and Zhang Xiaolin—fell on the Communist-led pickets and unions at dawn, and thousands died in the terror that followed. It is the hinge of this whole book: the moment the Shanghai gangs became instruments of the Nationalist state. Corroborated by all standard accounts.

The Cultural Revolution (1966–76), by its official PRC name (十年浩劫). Writing in 1986, the preface makes the era’s conventional move of tracing the gangs’ lingering ‘poison’ to Lin Biao (Mao’s designated heir, who died in 1971 fleeing an alleged coup) and the ‘Gang of Four’ (Jiang Qing and her allies, blamed after 1976 for the upheaval)—a rhetorical link, not a documented one.

The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom (太平天国, 1851–64), the vast religious-political rebellion against the Qing led by Hong Xiuquan, which convulsed south and central China at a cost of tens of millions of lives.

ch02.anchor: the recovery of Shanghai in the Revolution of 1911
ch02.note: In the Revolution of 1911 (the Xinhai Revolution) that ended the Qing dynasty, gang and secret-society forces helped wrest Shanghai from the imperial authorities in November 1911. ‘Recovery’ (光复) is the period word for a city’s passing out of Qing hands.

ch03.note: 1905–1996; the author. A postal clerk who rose through both the Green Gang and the Nationalist labour machine to chair the Shanghai General Labour Union, he broke with the Kuomintang in 1948, joined the new regime, and became a government minister and vice-chairman of the NPC Standing Committee—the official who also brushed this book’s title. His memoir is thus an insider’s account, written from within the establishment it describes.
1899–1967; a founding labour organizer of the Chinese Communist Party, a leader of the May Thirtieth Movement, and, in 1930, briefly its paramount leader (the ‘Li Lisan line’).
1898–1927; pioneer Communist labour organizer in Shanghai, active among the Pudong mill and dock workers; executed by the Nationalists in 1927.

The nationwide anti-imperialist upsurge touched off on 30 May 1925, when British-officered police in the Shanghai International Settlement shot dead demonstrators protesting the killing of a Chinese worker at a Japanese mill. It set off strikes and boycotts across China and was a turning point for the labour and revolutionary movements.

Anyuan, a colliery and rail town on the Hunan–Jiangxi border, was the site of a celebrated Communist-led miners’ and railwaymen’s movement in the early 1920s (Li Lisan and Liu Shaoqi among its organizers), in which the Party learned to work with—and through—the local secret societies.

ch03.anchor: the Rihua Cotton Mill in Pudong
ch03.note: The Rihua (Nihua) mill (日华纱厂), a Sino-Japanese cotton mill across the Huangpu in Pudong, was an early battleground of the Shanghai labour movement; the author cites its lost strike as a lesson in the gangs’ power.

A secure, lifelong livelihood; the metal bowl will not break as an earthenware one would. The author’s ranking—a customs post a ‘golden’ bowl, a bank post ‘silver,’ the post office ‘iron’—grades the era’s coveted salaried jobs by how secure each was thought to be.

‘Yellow’ unions (黄色工会), in the labour-movement vocabulary of the day, were the state- and employer-tolerated unions—here the Kuomintang-controlled bodies—as opposed to the Communist-led ‘red’ unions driven underground after 1927.

Entering a gang boss’s ‘door’ as a disciple (门生) meant a formal master-pupil bond, sealed by presenting a written pledge; it created lifelong obligations of protection upward and loyalty downward. The author, an educated union official, took Du Yuesheng as master purely for the leverage the tie conferred—a candour characteristic of this memoir.

ch03.anchor: constant as the moon in its fullness
ch03.note: The Heng Society’s name puns on Du Yuesheng: heng (恒, ‘constant’) evokes the phrase ‘constant as the moon at the full,’ while yue (月, ‘moon’) is the middle graph of Du’s given name Yuesheng. The society’s emblem—a bell (a homophone of sheng) beneath a new moon—spells the name a second way.

The ‘January Twenty-Eighth Incident’ of 1932: Japanese forces attacked the Zhabei district of Shanghai on 28 January and fought the Chinese 19th Route Army for weeks before a truce. It devastated the city’s northern industrial quarter and deepened the slump the author describes.

ch03.anchor: the December Ninth student movement in Beiping
ch03.note: The student demonstrations that began in Beiping (Beijing) on 9 December 1935, demanding resistance to Japanese encroachment in north China; they helped touch off the national salvation movement of 1935–37.

Funatsu Tatsuichirō (1873–1947), a Japanese diplomat and, in the 1930s, chairman of the association of Japanese cotton mills in China; his appeal to Du Yuesheng to mediate the 1936 general strike measures the gang boss’s standing with foreign capital.
‘White’ Russians—émigrés who had fled the Bolshevik revolution—formed a large, often destitute community in Shanghai and were a ready pool of strike-breakers and armed guards for foreign firms.

Chiang’s statement at the Lushan hill resort in mid-July 1937, after the Marco Polo Bridge clash, declaring that China would fight if pushed to ‘the last extremity’—widely taken as the Nationalist government’s commitment to full resistance against Japan.

During the Battle of Shanghai (August–November 1937), Du Yuesheng and Dai Li’s secret service armed irregular units (别动队) drawn largely from Green Gang and Hongmen men and from workers; the author commanded one of the five detachments. Poorly armed and barely used, they were disbanded when the city fell.

ch03.anchor: After Shanghai became a solitary island
ch03.note: The ‘solitary island’ (孤岛) period: after the Chinese city fell in November 1937, the foreign concessions kept a precarious neutral existence, an island of unoccupied ground ringed by Japanese-held territory, until Japan seized them after Pearl Harbor in December 1941.
Xiang Songpo, better known as Xiang Haiqian (1888–1974): a leader of the Hongmen’s ‘Five Lakes’ lodges and a 1911 revolutionary, who used the brotherhoods for anti-Japanese organizing in this period.

Lu Liankui, former chief detective inspector of the International Settlement police, and Lu Bohong (Joseph Lo Pa Hong), a prominent Catholic industrialist who headed a Japanese-sponsored ‘maintenance’ body—both assassinated as collaborators early in the occupation. The author’s claim that his hidden pistols were the weapons used is his own; the killings themselves are attested.

ch04.note: The author; a Communist underground worker who from the 1920s to the 1940s ran united-front work with gang and secret-society figures in Beijing and Shanghai. His account is a rare inside record of how the Party used the gangs—candid about the transactional nature of the ties.

From Mao Zedong’s Analysis of the Classes in Chinese Society (1925). The passage on the ‘lumpen-proletariat’ and its secret societies—quoted here to license the Party’s use of the gangs—was among the lines Mao softened in later editions of his Selected Works.
1884–1951; also Hu Nanhu. A 1911 revolutionary and Beiyang education official who joined the Communist Party in the 1920s and worked its united front among old revolutionaries and gang figures.

Yang Du (1875–1931): the classical scholar who had once championed monarchy under Yuan Shikai, then joined the Communist Party in secret in 1929 while serving as an adviser to Du Yuesheng—a startling double life the Party did not confirm publicly until 1975. The book’s account of his role is broadly corroborated.

1889–1927; co-founder of the Chinese Communist Party. In April 1927 Zhang Zuolin’s troops raided the Soviet embassy compound in Beijing’s Legation Quarter, where he had taken refuge, and hanged him—the event this passage describes.

Lev Karakhan (1889–1937), Soviet deputy foreign commissar and ambassador to China in the mid-1920s, known for the ‘Karakhan Manifesto’ renouncing Tsarist privileges. He was executed in Stalin’s purges.

The walled diplomatic quarter of Beijing, established after 1901, where the foreign legations—including the Soviet embassy—enjoyed extraterritorial protection; Zhang Zuolin’s 1927 raid on the Soviet compound there breached that immunity.

The Mutual Aid Society (互济会) was the Chinese branch of International Red Aid, a Comintern body that supported jailed revolutionaries and their families. The organizer’s name is uncertain in the scan and is romanized here provisionally as Dai Xiaodong.
1889–1971; geologist and senior Nationalist official, acting president of Tsinghua University in 1931 and later premier; he returned to the mainland in 1951.

1882–1948; the ‘Christian general,’ a warlord whose loyalties shifted among the Nationalists, the Soviets, and the left. In 1933, with Communist help, he raised the short-lived Chahar People’s Anti-Japanese Allied Army at Zhangjiakou, into which the local forces described here were folded.

1915–1968; a Nationalist air-force bomber pilot who defected by flying his aircraft to the Communist base at Yan’an. His defection is dated June 1946 in the standard accounts; the article’s ‘1947’ appears to be a slip of memory.

76 Jessfield Road (极司非尔路, today Wanhangdu Road) was the headquarters of the secret service of the puppet Wang Jingwei regime, notorious for torture and assassination; its address became a synonym for the collaborationist terror apparatus.

1907–2000; Buddhist lay leader, poet, and relief organizer who used Shanghai’s charitable and refugee bodies to shelter and channel Communist work in the war years, and later headed the Buddhist Association of China. The refugee network he built here fed cadres to the New Fourth Army, as the article claims.

The Communist force operating in central and east China after 1937 under the united front, alongside the northern Eighth Route Army; the refugee schools and radio classes described here were among its recruiting grounds until the Nationalists attacked it in the 1941 New Fourth Army Incident.

The ‘Jiang-kang’ (江抗), an early Communist-influenced guerrilla force built in the Yangtze delta from local gang levies; reorganized under regular military command, it fed into the New Fourth Army’s eastward push.
1885–1961; a well-known Shanghai gang figure with revolutionary sympathies, treated at length in a later article of this volume.

ch05.anchor: *tongcao* handbooks that circulate within the gang
ch05.note: Author’s note. The tongcao are also written 通潦, 通钮, or 统抄 (all pronounced roughly tongcao), secret handbooks internal to the gang. The editions are many; I have seen more than thirty in print or manuscript. Their contents amount to records of the Green Gang’s successive patriarchs, the grain-boat system, gang rules, ritual observances, argot, and the like—mostly a cobbled-together jumble, but preserving some of the gang’s own original material.

ch05.anchor: the Qing grain-tribute transport
ch05.note: The caoyun, the state system that shipped grain levied as land tax from the provinces to the capital, chiefly along the Grand Canal; it employed hundreds of thousands of boatmen and was the seedbed of the Green Gang. The grain was measured in dan or piculs (here ‘piculs’), a unit of about 100 catties, roughly 60 kilograms.

ch05.anchor: the founder of the Luo sect
ch05.note: Patriarch Luo (Luo Menghong, c. 1442–1527) founded the lay-Buddhist Luo or ‘Non-Action’ sect, whose scriptures and hermitages spread widely among the grain-boat crews. Li Shiyu argues below that the Green Gang grew out of this milieu but was not simply a branch of the Luo sect.

ch05.anchor: ranked, by the order in which they entered, into twenty-four generations
ch05.note: The generation-characters are the key to Green Gang rank. Each member belonged to one of the twenty-four generations, named in fixed order by the characters of the verse; seniority ran by generation, not by age or wealth, so that a man of an earlier character outranked all of a later one. Thus of the late bosses, Zhang Renkui was of the ‘Da’ generation, Huang Jinrong of the ‘Tong,’ and Du Yuesheng of the ‘Wu’—Du being, in strict gang terms, junior to the other two.

ch05.anchor: the Boxers' turn from
ch05.note: The Yihetuan or ‘Boxers,’ whose 1900 anti-foreign rising began under the slogan ‘overthrow the Qing’ but shifted to ‘support the Qing, destroy the foreigner’ as the court took them up—the parallel Li Shiyu draws for the gang’s passage from ‘Anqing’ to ‘An-Qing’ (‘pacify the Qing’).

ch05.anchor: a branch of the White Lotus
ch05.note: The White Lotus (Bailianjiao) was a broad family of millenarian sects, repeatedly rising against the Qing; several risings named here—Wang Lun’s Clear Water sect, the Eight Trigrams, the Sichuan–Hubei–Shaanxi rising—belonged to this tradition.

ch06.note: This whole patriarchal genealogy—the ‘Former’ and ‘Latter’ Three Patriarchs—is gang legend, not history. Jin Youzi (1368–1431) was a real Ming Grand Secretary but had nothing to do with any gang; ‘Luo Qing’ conflates him with Patriarch Luo of the Luo sect. As Li Shiyu’s study (the preceding chapter) shows from the archives, the Green Gang in fact took shape among the grain-transport boatmen in the early Yongzheng years. Jiang Hao here sets down the gang’s own account of itself.

ch06.anchor: Tian Wenjing, was a Hangzhou man
ch06.note: Tian Wenjing (1662–1732) was a real and prominent Yongzheng-era governor of Henan; the gang legend attaches its founding to his sponsorship of a grain-transport reform.

The Eight Immortals, the twenty-eight lunar mansions, the thirty-six Heavenly Stars, and the seventy-two Earthly Fiends are stock numbers of Chinese cosmology and popular fiction (the thirty-six and seventy-two are the number of the bandit-heroes of Water Margin); the legend borrows them for the founders’ first intakes of disciples.

The Juntong (军统), the Nationalists’ Bureau of Investigation and Statistics, the Kuomintang secret service run by Dai Li. The English form is not yet settled across this series and is treated fully at the chapter on Du Yuesheng’s ties to Dai Li; here it is rendered ‘the Juntong.’

ch06.anchor: his organization was called the Yi Society, and in the Hongmen he was lord of the Wuxing Mountain lodge
ch06.note: Several minor Shanghai clubs bore near-homophonous names all rendered ‘Yi Society’ here: Zhu Xuefan’s 毅社 (Chapter 3), Xu Yimin’s 逸社, and Sun Yixiang’s 怔社—distinct bodies that happen to sound alike.

ch06.anchor: one of the "Three Big Bosses" among the Shanghai gangsters
ch06.note: The ‘Three Big Bosses’ (san da heng) of the Shanghai underworld—Huang Jinrong, Zhang Xiaolin, and Du Yuesheng—the trio around whom much of this book turns.
The ‘Mandarin Duck and Butterfly’ school was a popular current of sentimental and romantic fiction in early-Republican Shanghai, looked down on by the new-literature writers.
No. 76 Jessfield Road was the notorious headquarters of the secret service of the puppet Wang Jingwei regime during the occupation, a byword for terror and torture.
Kawashima Yoshiko (1907–1948), a Manchu Qing princess raised in Japan who worked as a Japanese agent; executed as a traitor after the war.

ch06.anchor: the noted film actress Ruan Lingyu
ch06.note: Ruan Lingyu (1910–1935), one of the great stars of Shanghai silent film, whose suicide at twenty-four was a national sensation.
Silas Aaron Hardoon (1851–1931), a Baghdadi-Jewish property magnate, reputedly the richest foreigner in Shanghai; his wife Luo Jialing (Liza Hardoon) was Eurasian.
The ‘CC Clique,’ the Kuomintang organizational faction led by the brothers Chen Guofu and Chen Lifu, a mainstay of anti-Communist party control.
